title: Young of domestic breeds differ much less than adults

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Young of domestic breeds differ much less than adults

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The characteristic differences between domestic breeds produced by man's selection (in dogs, horses and pigeons) generally do not appear early in life and are inherited at a corresponding later age, so that the young of different breeds differ far less in proportions than the adults, with occasional exceptions such as the short-faced tumbler pigeon.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: the characteristic differences which give value to each breed, and which have been accumulated by man’s selection, have not generally first appeared at an early period of life, and have been inherited by the offspring at a corresponding not early period.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XIII, “Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs”; section “EMBRYOLOGY, laws of, explained by variations not supervening at an early age, and being inherited at a corresponding age”. Scope: domestic breeds of dogs, horses and pigeons

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch13-18: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.63

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The age-by-breed disparity prediction is direct and strongly discriminating. Data exist for subsets and individual studies, but a full three-species test requires substantial compilation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For multiple breeds of dogs, horses and pigeons, quantify standardized body-shape disparity at matched juvenile and adult ages and test whether between-breed disparity increases with age. Developmental timing of breed-associated alleles can separately test corresponding-age expression.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Breed standards and management alter growth trajectories.

Longitudinal, age-matched morphology is not harmonized across the three domestic species.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The age contrast in proportions is directly measurable and would clearly confirm or refute the claim for these three domesticated species. The obstacle is data organization: published growth series would have to be compiled study by study, and they cover some dog and horse breeds far better than a balanced sample of pigeon breeds. That is a restricted, paper-by-paper test rather than an analysis of an existing public dataset.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For dog, horse and pigeon breeds, compare multivariate distances among breeds at neonatal or juvenile stages and at adulthood on the same landmarks, excluding or separately noting early-appearing exceptions such as the short-faced tumbler. The claim is confirmed if among-breed distance increases with age for the breed-diagnostic proportions, and refuted if neonates already differ as much as adults across those breeds.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Body size and allometry change proportions within a breed as it grows, and must be separated from true among-breed divergence.

Age-by-breed measurements exist as scattered veterinary and pigeon studies, not as one open morphometric table.

Breed standards and show data describe adults, so the juvenile half has to be recovered from separate growth papers.

fields.value:

analysis feasibility: 0.35
operationalizability: 0.85
discriminating power: 0.7
